content: 1. The diagnosis of pregnancy is crucial, and the ability to confirm pregnancy early depends on the resources and settings available. Biochemical pregnancy tests, which are highly reliable, are often helpful but may not be accessible in all areas. Pelvic examination, when feasible, is reliable approximately 8–10 weeks after the first day of the last menstrual period. A healthcare provider can reasonably confirm that a woman is not pregnant if she has no symptoms or signs of pregnancy and meets specific criteria, such as no intercourse since her last normal menses, consistent use of a reliable contraceptive method, being within the first 7 days after normal menses, within 4 weeks postpartum (for non-lactating women), within 7 days post-abortion or miscarriage, or fully or nearly fully breastfeeding, amenorrheic, and less than six months postpartum. 2. Intrauterine devices (IUDs) are long-acting contraceptive methods suitable for most women, including adolescents and nulliparous women. To determine if women with certain medical conditions or characteristics can safely use IUDs, refer to the Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, Fifth Edition. IUDs do not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV. If there is a risk of STI/HIV, consistent and correct condom use is recommended. Condoms, when used correctly, are among the most effective methods for STI protection. Female condoms are also effective and safe but are less widely used than male condoms. 3. Copper-bearing IUDs (Cu-IUDs) and levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs (LNG-IUDs) can be initiated under specific conditions. For Cu-IUDs, they can be inserted within 12 days of the start of menstrual bleeding without additional contraceptive protection. If more than 12 days have passed, insertion is possible if pregnancy can be reasonably excluded. For LNG-IUDs, they can be inserted within 7 days of the start of menstrual bleeding without additional protection. If more than 7 days have passed, the woman must abstain from sex or use additional contraception for the next 7 days. 4. Postpartum IUD insertion is possible within 48 hours after delivery, including immediately after placental delivery. For cesarean deliveries, the IUD can be placed after placental delivery but before uterine closure. Between 48 hours and less than 4 weeks postpartum, IUD use is generally not recommended unless other methods are unavailable or unacceptable. After 4 weeks postpartum, IUDs can be inserted if pregnancy can be excluded. Women with puerperal sepsis should not have an IUD inserted. 5. Post-abortion IUD insertion is generally safe immediately after a firstor second-trimester abortion. However, IUDs should not be inserted immediately following a septic abortion. 6. Switching from another contraceptive method to an IUD can be done immediately if pregnancy can be excluded. For LNG-IUDs, if the previous method was an injectable contraceptive, the IUD should be inserted when the repeat injection would have been due. 7. For emergency contraception, a Cu-IUD can be inserted within 5 days of unprotected intercourse. If ovulation timing can be estimated, insertion beyond 5 days is possible as long as it occurs no more than 5 days after ovulation. LNG-IUDs are not recommended for emergency contraception due to unknown safety and effectiveness. 8. Before IUD insertion, essential examinations include a pelvic/genital examination and STI risk assessment. Optional but beneficial tests include hemoglobin testing and STI/HIV screening. Prophylactic antibiotics are generally not recommended for routine IUD insertion, except in settings with high STI prevalence and limited screening. 9. Menstrual abnormalities, such as spotting or light bleeding, are common during the first 3–6 months of Cu-IUD use. These are usually harmless and decrease over time. Treatment with NSAIDs during bleeding days may help. Persistent bleeding should prompt evaluation for gynecologic problems. If no issues are found and the bleeding is unacceptable, the IUD can be removed, and another method chosen. 10. Heavier or prolonged menstrual bleeding is also common during the first 3–6 months of Cu-IUD use. This typically resolves over time. Treatment options include NSAIDs or tranexamic acid, but aspirin should not be used. If bleeding remains heavy or prolonged, especially with signs of anemia, the IUD should be removed, and another method considered. Iron supplementation or dietary advice may help prevent anemia.
